draft.title: Keeping verb tense consistent
card: Tense shows when something happens. Past tense is for things that already happened, such as walked. Present tense is for things happening now, such as walks.
A writer picks one tense for a piece of writing and sticks to it. A story told in the past tense keeps its verbs in the past tense.
A mistake happens when the verbs slip into another tense for no reason. Example: "Ravi opened the gate and walks inside." Opened is past, but walks is present.
A writer may change tense when the time really changes. Example: "Ravi was nervous, but now he feels calm." The words but now show a shift from the past to the present.
draft.remember: Stay in one tense unless the time changes. Do not slip by accident.

a.q: Which sentence keeps its verbs in the same tense?
opts: Lena packed her bag and left for school
Lena packed her bag and leaves for school
Lena packs her bag and left for school
Lena packs her bag and walked to school
a.why: Packed and left are both past tense, so the sentence stays consistent. The second option is tempting because it reads smoothly, but it mixes past packed with present leaves for no reason.
a.clue: Check that both verbs show the same time.

b.q: Tom writes a story in the past tense: "Mia climbed the hill. Then she sees the sea and smiled." Which verb is the mistake?
opts: sees, because it is present in a past tense story
climbed, because the climbing has finished
smiled, because it is the last verb in the story
Then, because it starts the second sentence
b.why: The story is told in the past tense, so sees should be saw. Climbed and smiled are both past tense and fit the story. Climbed is not wrong just because the climbing has finished.
b.clue: Find the one verb that does not show the past.
